subject: economics
title: Labour Demand and Supply
welcome_lead: Wages are a price like any other - determined by demand and supply.
meta_desc: A-Level Labour Markets: derived demand, supply of labour.
final_note: Wages reflect productivity, working conditions and barriers to mobility.

concepts.def: Labour demand depends on demand for output.
Marginal Revenue Product - extra revenue from an extra worker.
Workers willing to work at each wage.
Pay gap between groups or roles.
Total package: wages plus non-monetary benefits.
Ability of workers to move between locations.

walkthroughs.body_html: Firms hire while MRP exceeds the wage. As more workers join, diminishing returns lower MRP, so the labour demand curve slopes down.
Higher wages attract more workers - but at very high incomes some prefer leisure (backward-bending supply). Supply also depends on training time, demographics and migration.
Differentials reflect skill, risk, working conditions and barriers. Compensating differentials pay danger premiums; barriers to entry (medicine) keep wages high.

mcqs.q: Labour demand is described as derived because:
options: Workers derive incomes from it
It depends on demand for the output produced
It is always inelastic
It equals MRP

mcqs.q: Diminishing MRP makes the labour demand curve:
options: Vertical
Slope downwards
Slope upwards
Horizontal

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.
Demand always falls when supply increases.

mcqs.q: What does standard theory predict about a minimum wage?
options: A minimum wage always reduces unemployment because workers have more money to spend.
A minimum wage is paid by the government.
Demand always falls when supply increases.
If above equilibrium, it raises wages for those still employed but causes unemployment by reducing labour demand — though empirical evidence is mixed.

mcqs.q: What causes the supply curve to shift?
options: Changes in production costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of producers, expectations — anything affecting supply other than the good's own price.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
A minimum wage is paid by the government.
When demand rises, the supply curve shifts right to meet it.
